title: My difficulty checker said a stage had a 0.002% success rate. A person solved it in three tries. Why I placed all 100 stages of my gravity puzzle by hand
author: office-canard
selftext:
PROBE GRAVITY is a gravity puzzle. You launch a probe, and the planets around it bend its path. Red planets pull, blue ones push. Read every pull at once, find the one line through, and bring the probe home to Earth.



What's standing between you and Earth is gravity, and what gets you there is gravity too. You can't fly straight, so the only way through is to ride the pull that's throwing you off. The obstacle and the tool are the same thing.



I usually make endless games, with stages generated on the fly. I tried that here too. Then something strange kept happening.



How AI fit in:

Claude wrote all of the code, including the physics, which is fairly rigorous. It also built a harness that measures difficulty by brute force: it fires shots across every aim and timing and counts how many reach Earth, so a generator could grade its own stages.



The harness works. But its numbers and the way a stage actually feels didn't match. Not slightly, wildly. It would rate a layout at 0.002%, and then a person would solve it in three tries.



It took me a while to see why. Because the physics is honest, the probe curves the way real things curve. Nobody has been to space, but we've all spent our lives watching things fall and swing and arc. Your body already knows how it should bend. The machine computes every shot from zero. It has no body, so it never sees that coming.



So I placed all 100 stages by hand. It isn't a defeat. 100 is just where it rests for now. From 101 on, the distance to Earth gets longer, so it would become less a puzzle tightening and more a journey stretching out.
